Or perhaps not. That is, perhaps not that night, or those words (if not Sabine's voluble, distracted and inept chat¬ ter), that exit. Perhaps merely, instead of that, a few glances (or not even that: eyes avoiding all meetings), words withheld, or spoken another time, or perhaps never spoken, only thought, and not an incident (the scandal, the uproar) occurring on a specific day, but something latent, something permanent, established, the other scene which Louise could also see again afterwards, belonging too, perhaps, to that domain of the latent, the inexpressed, or—the limit, the line of demarcation between the formu¬ lated and the unformulated consisting only of this porous, clumsy and fragile barrier of words—perhaps not. A little later, in their room (that is, the room which was theirs not because they (Louise and Georges) had furnished it, decorated it, arranged it to suit their tastes—except for two or three objects and a chest from her room as a girl— but theirs only because the fact of sleeping and making love between four walls (whatever they are, even those of a venal hotel bedroom) over a long enough period finally confers upon them, as on the flowers of the wallpaper and the anonymous furniture, that emollient characteristic of servile and contemptible complicity, intimate, reassuring and yet tyrannical, which, as well as what we have ac¬ quired by money or by choice, is equivalent to a deed of 126 ownership, with all that the concept of possession involves with regard to servitudes, subjection, and submission), in their room, then, Louise lying on the unopened bed, still dressed, the smoke of her cigarette rising, coiling and un¬ coiling in front of the dark window-frame, and the voice reaching her from the bathroom through the open door, mingling with the purifying sound of water, saying: . . because I wish Ld never read a book, never touched a book in my life, I wish I never even knew such a thing as a book existed, I wish I could not even know, I mean have learned, I mean have let myself learn, have been stupid enough to believe the people who taught me that letters lined up on white paper could mean something be¬ sides letters on white paper, I mean exactly nothing, ex¬ cept as a distraction, a way of killing time, and for people like him an excuse for showing off.
